speaker: John Carmack
title: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets (#309)
question: In consumer virtual reality, why have simple arcade-style rhythm games consistently outperformed realistic open-world exploration games?
guest: It makes very clear sense when you analyze the engineering reasons. So many things you do with VR controllers break the illusion—like trying to pick up glasses where you hit a grip button when you're close and it snaps into your hand. Those are unnatural actions. A game like Beat Saber plays only to VR's strengths and completely hides its weaknesses: you keep a solid grip on a controller the whole time, and you have a lightsaber that slices through things without ever bumping into anything. You never reach the point where you knock on a table and your hand passes right through it, because you expect a lightsaber to slice through everything. Audio and music are also hugely powerful when you're blocking the outside world off. And unlike modern games with hour-long tutorials, VR still has locomotion comfort issues, headset wear discomfort, and mobile battery limits. Breaking gameplay into three- and four-minute loops while you stand still and everything flies at you avoids motion sickness and turns out to be a perfect storm for VR.

points.core: Realistic object manipulation breaks immersion because VR controllers lack physical collision resistance.
points.note: Accept: hands passing through solid virtual surfaces or unnatural button-snapping to grab objects shatter the illusion of physical interaction. Do not credit: generic complaints about bad VR graphics or clunky menus.

points.core: Slicing mechanics hide missing haptics because players naturally expect zero physical stopping resistance.
points.note: Accept: holding a constant grip on a blade or lightsaber that cuts cleanly through targets aligns with user expectations so the brain never expects tactile pushback. Do not credit: vague statements that rhythm games are more fun or accessible.

points.core: Keeping players stationary while incoming targets approach eliminates virtual locomotion motion sickness.
points.note: Accept: avoiding artificial movement through 3D worlds prevents VR comfort issues and nausea that plague exploration games. Do not credit: mentioning VR comfort generically without contrasting stationary play against locomotion.

points.core: Short multi-minute gameplay loops accommodate standalone VR headset comfort limits far better.
points.note: Accept: 3–4 minute sessions fit physical headset wear discomfort or mobile battery lifespan, unlike hour-long console tutorials or RPG sessions. Do not credit: generic claims that casual gamers have short attention spans.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Rhythm games like Beat Saber fit the medium's constraints, while realistic open worlds fight them.

The biggest factor is comfort. Rhythm games keep the player stationary, so what the eyes see matches what the inner ear feels. Open-world exploration needs artificial locomotion, which causes motion sickness in many users and limits session length.

Hardware matters too. Most headsets sold are standalone devices running mobile-class chips, such as the Quest. Stylized, abstract visuals run at high, stable frame rates, whereas realistic open worlds look compromised or demand an expensive PC.

Session shape also favors arcade design. Headsets are heavy, warm and isolating, so people prefer short, repeatable bursts, not multi-hour campaigns. Rhythm games are instantly understandable, easy to demo to friends, good exercise, and endlessly replayable through new songs and score chasing.

Finally, economics: the VR install base is small, so high-budget open worlds rarely recoup their costs, while small teams can build polished rhythm games cheaply and sustain them with music DLC.

The premise holds mainly for sales; ambitious titles like Half-Life: Alyx and Skyrim VR did succeed critically and sold reasonably well.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Simple arcade-style rhythm games like *Beat Saber* outperform realistic open worlds in consumer virtual reality because they embrace the medium's ergonomic, technical, and economic realities rather than fighting them. Stationary gameplay eliminates artificial locomotion, preventing the motion sickness that alienates casual players during virtual exploration. Meanwhile, standalone headsets running mobile processors dominate the consumer market; stylized, contained environments easily maintain the high, stable frame rates essential for VR comfort, whereas realistic open worlds demand expensive PC hardware or suffer steep visual compromises. Wearing a headset also causes physical fatigue, favoring brisk, high-energy sessions and immediate kinesthetic feedback over multi-hour traversal and complex menus. Furthermore, intuitive physical mechanics require zero gaming literacy, double as fitness routines, and create clear spectator appeal that drives mainstream word-of-mouth adoption. Finally, VR's relatively modest install base rarely justifies the massive budgets required for AAA open-world production, allowing polished, endlessly replayable arcade experiences to dominate both studio investment and consumer sales.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because rhythm games fit what consumer VR hardware and its users handle well, though the premise needs a caveat. Beat Saber is one of VR's best-selling games, but social titles like Gorilla Tag and Rec Room have drawn bigger audiences, and realistic games such as Half-Life: Alyx and Skyrim VR have also sold well.

The biggest factor is comfort. Moving smoothly through a large open world with a thumbstick while your body stands still causes motion sickness in many people. A rhythm game keeps you in one spot, so that conflict between what you see and what you feel never happens.

Hardware matters too. Standalone headsets like the Quest run on mobile chips that struggle with big, detailed worlds at the high frame rates VR needs. Simple arcade graphics run smoothly on them.

Session length counts as well. Headsets get heavy and hot after a while, so short 3-to-5-minute songs suit how people actually use them better than multi-hour exploring.

Finally, swinging at blocks to music shows off hand tracking right away, needs no tutorial, and works as exercise and as something fun to watch at parties. That word of mouth helped sales.

The response explicitly links artificial locomotion to motion sickness and explains how stationary play avoids the sensory conflict.

A rhythm game keeps you in one spot, so that conflict between what you see and what you feel never happens.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Simple arcade-style rhythm games outperform realistic open-world titles in consumer VR because they align naturally with the medium's physical, technical, and market realities. First, keeping the player stationary or moving predictably avoids the artificial locomotion that triggers motion sickness for many users during free-roaming exploration. Second, because mainstream VR relies heavily on standalone headsets with mobile-class processors, clean, stylized visuals can run effortlessly at the high frame rates needed for comfort, whereas realistic open worlds often suffer from compromised graphics and performance. Third, wearing a headset can be physically fatiguing and isolating, making short, pick-up-and-play sessions far more appealing than multi-hour narratives. Rhythm games also require almost no learning curve—anyone can immediately grasp swinging to a beat—which gives them broad appeal among casual players, partygoers, and fitness enthusiasts. Finally, open-world games demand massive budgets that rarely recoup costs in VR's relatively small install base, while focused arcade experiences deliver high replayability at a sustainable development scale.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Arcade rhythm games like Beat Saber turn VR’s strengths into something players can enjoy within seconds. Swinging tracked controllers to music feels natural, the beat tells players when to move, and each hit gives immediate feedback. A song lasts a few minutes, and higher scores, harder charts, and favorite tracks give players a reason to return. Because players generally stay in one spot, these games also avoid much of the motion sickness that can come from moving a virtual camera while the player’s body stays still.

Realistic open worlds ask more of both the player and the hardware. Traversal, menus, and inventory can be awkward in a headset, and long play sessions can become physically tiring. Detailed worlds are expensive to build and must sustain the high, stable frame rates that keep VR comfortable, especially on standalone headsets. Rhythm games can deliver their core appeal with simpler visuals and a smaller production budget, making it easier to reach a broad audience and earn repeat play.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Arcade-style rhythm games turn a small play space into an advantage. In Beat Saber, you can stand in one spot, swing your hands, and immediately see, hear, and feel whether you hit the beat. A newcomer can understand the game in seconds, while harder songs and high scores give experienced players a reason to return. A single song also fits a short headset session.

Realistic open worlds can be compelling, but their main appeal is traveling through a large place. Few players have room to walk far, joystick movement can cause motion sickness, and teleportation can interrupt the feeling of a continuous journey. Detailed worlds are also expensive to build and harder to render smoothly on standalone headsets. Those differences help explain rhythm games’ broad appeal, though “consistently outperformed” depends on whether you mean sales, player retention, or critical reception.
